extracted.intended_audience: physicians, medical historians, and educated general readers interested in historical medical diagnosis (Dean Swift / otology)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate historical case evidence (letters, journals, autopsy/cast) to determine whether Dean Swift's lifelong complaints correspond to labyrinthine vertigo (Meniere's disease). Focus is on symptom patterns, course, and anatomical/experimental corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic symptoms of labyrinthine vertigo (Meniere)
rubrics_metrics.description: "that the patient is suddenly seized with vertigo and a feeling of nausea or positive sickness, with great constitutional depression and faintness. Usually the giddiness comes on simultaneously with ringing or buzzing in one or, it may be, both ears."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These clustered symptoms (paroxysmal vertigo + nausea + tinnitus + constitutional disturbance) are the core diagnostic triad offered in the text; the author repeatedly cites Swift's journals and letters showing fits of giddiness with sickness and ear-noise as primary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two recognized clinical forms of the disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation of Fere: "une forme grave avec etat vertigineux a peu pres permanent interrompu par les paroxysmes, et une forme moins facheuse, constitue par des acces separes par des periodes de sante parfaite."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between (a) a severe form with near-permanent vertiginous state punctuated by paroxysms and (b) a benign form with separated attacks and long symptom-free intervals. Swift is considered an example of the benign form (remissions sometimes many months).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paroxysmal/periodic course with variable frequency and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: The disease is paroxysmal in nature, with attacks that may be infrequent or frequent; attacks in Swift's record sometimes lasted about three weeks, and remissions could be long (one cited remission of eleven months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for documentation of discrete 'fits' or attacks in correspondence/journals, their duration (days–weeks), and intervals of apparent health; note that even brief attacks could produce prolonged constitutional debility ('a little turn... made me as weak as a dog all this day').

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistent hearing loss and subjective auditory symptoms between attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: In the benign form "la surdite persiste avec une intensite variable, et elle s'accompagne souvent des sensations subjectives intermittentes de l'ouie."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis supports labyrinthine origin when deafness/tinnitus persist between paroxysms and are variable rather than absent; persistent unilateral/bilateral ear symptoms accompanying vertigo favor Meniere's diagnosis over other vertiginous causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triggering by head movement and extreme sensitivity to slight movement
rubrics_metrics.description: A characteristic noted in Swift's case: "at one time any slight movement of the head brought it on."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation that small or sudden head turns precipitate vertigo episodes is an important supportive feature pointing to vestibular (semicircular canal) involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing labyrinthine vertigo from cerebral or stomachic vertigo
rubrics_metrics.description: The author notes Swift distinguished 'ordinary' from 'vertiginous' headache and records: 'My head is pretty well; only a sudden turn at any time makes me feel giddy for a moment, and sometimes it feels very stuffed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of ear-related symptoms (tinnitus, deafness) and rotatory sensation with head-movement-provocation argues for a peripheral (labyrinthine) cause rather than central (cerebral) or gastric origins of giddiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional and neuropsychiatric sequelae
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated attacks produce 'great constitutional depression and faintness' and over years are associated with irritability, melancholy, memory impairment and, eventually, profound mental decline in advanced stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the long-term systemic and mental effects as part of the illness course (e.g., progressive depression, irritability, impaired memory); however, the author cautions that early/longstanding physical disease does not necessarily imply primary insanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disease duration tied to progression of deafness
rubrics_metrics.description: "La maladie elle-meme dure tant que la surdite n'est pas absolute."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents the notion that the disease persists until deafness becomes absolute; thus progressive hearing loss signals ongoing disease activity and may mark disease endpoint in classical descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental/etiological support linking semicircular canal pathology to vertigo
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to Fleurens's experiments on the semicircular canals of pigeons and rabbits and Meniere's recognition (1861) of the causal connection between auditory organ lesions and vertigo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experimental animal evidence and physiological understanding (semicircular canals as the vestibular organ) as etiologic support when interpreting historical symptom reports as labyrinthine in origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical/post-mortem observations as supportive but limited evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Autopsy note: 'opened the skull, and found much water in the brain.' Cast findings (Wilde) include 'enormous development of the vessels within the cranium, the very small anterior lobes, the great size of the glandulae Pacchionian, the exceedingly small cerebellum... and the absence of any appearance of disease in the anterior lobes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morphological findings (brain 'water', skull/cast abnormalities) may be recorded and can be suggestive, but the author treats them cautiously; such anatomical observations should be correlated with clinical history rather than used alone to make the retrospective diagnosis.
